lesson.title: The Four Quadrants: Reading a Point's Neighborhood from Its Signs
lesson.summary: The x-axis and y-axis divide the coordinate plane into four quadrants, and the signs of a point's coordinates alone reveal which quadrant it lives in.
lesson.body:
Once the horizontal axis and vertical axis are drawn crossing at the origin, they slice the coordinate plane into four separate regions. These regions are called quadrants, and they are numbered using Roman numerals I through IV, starting in the upper right and moving counterclockwise. This numbering direction is a standing convention in mathematics, the same rotational direction used later for angles measured on the unit circle, so it is worth learning it correctly from the start rather than guessing each time a problem comes up.

Each quadrant corresponds to a unique combination of signs for the x-coordinate and y-coordinate, and that combination is really all you need to identify where a point lives without drawing anything at all. Quadrant I holds points where both coordinates are positive (+, +), sitting up and to the right of the origin. Quadrant II holds points where x is negative but y is positive (-, +), up and to the left. Quadrant III holds points where both coordinates are negative (-, -), down and to the left. Quadrant IV holds points where x is positive but y is negative (+, -), down and to the right. Memorizing this sign pattern turns quadrant identification into a quick mental check rather than a task that requires sketching a graph. Some students find it helpful to picture the four quadrants as a clock face turned into a cross, with Quadrant I in the upper right acting as the starting point each time the numbering sweeps counterclockwise around the origin.

Here is a worked example classifying four points using only their signs. The point (3, 5) has a positive x-coordinate and a positive y-coordinate, so it belongs in Quadrant I. The point (-2, 4) has a negative x-coordinate and a positive y-coordinate, placing it in Quadrant II. The point (-6, -1) has both coordinates negative, placing it in Quadrant III. The point (7, -3) has a positive x-coordinate and a negative y-coordinate, placing it in Quadrant IV. Notice that no calculation was needed at all, just a careful reading of two signs, which makes this one of the fastest checks available once coordinates are known.

Points that fall exactly on an axis are a special case worth flagging: they do not belong to any quadrant. A point like (0, 6) sits on the vertical axis, and a point like (-4, 0) sits on the horizontal axis, and the origin (0, 0) sits at the meeting point of all four regions. Quadrants only classify points that are strictly off both axes, with two nonzero coordinates, so it is worth checking for a zero coordinate before assigning a quadrant label at all.

Recognizing quadrants quickly becomes a useful checking tool once you start plotting points and graphing lines. If you calculate a point's coordinates and expect it to land in a particular quadrant based on the signs, but your plotted point lands somewhere else, that mismatch is an immediate signal to go back and check your arithmetic before moving on to the next step of a problem.
